chapter: Buck and Bubbles: Nazarro and Bubbles
title: Playing the Bones and the origin of thigh slapping
summary: The interviewers ask about the slapping of thighs in Bubbles' dance; Green traces it to Scotland and Ireland and compares it to Hambone.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Describe that dance to me, Chuck. What were you doing there? What -- describe how Bubbles utilized the different steps and how he slapped his --
-- his thighs. What were all those things?

Well, he called that part of the Bone, you know, that -- the slapping of the thighs and the hands, it's called Bones, you know, Playing the Bones, you see. And -- but he inserted it into the tap dancing. While tap dancing, he inserted it into a rhythmical pattern, and it would be a part of the rhythm, of the step he's doing.
Excuse me. How -- how far back do you think that goes with the (unintelligible)? Do you think that's, you know, like Africans do a lot of that too, you know. I don't know. Would that be --

Yeah, well, I think that's handed down from Scotland. I think it's handed down from Scotland. They have a dance they call -- well, it was reinstated here in America, got into the folk dance, called square dancing, where they, you know -- wuh-uh-uh -- what they call it? Yeah, that's square dancing. Yeah. And that's where they use -- but I'm quite sure it's mostly from Scotland and Ireland. The Irish --
The slapping of the thighs and --

Yeah, that's some kind of -- where they beat the bottom of the foot too, you see. That's into it, inserted into it, where they clap their hands, and it became a novelty style of performing, entertaining, where they used to take two spoons and turn the spoons back to back and play the spoons like they did sticks, you know, and they call that Bones, Playing Bones, you know.
Well, down South there's a thing called Hambones.
Slapping of the knees, which a lot of people still --a lot of kids still do down South.
Yeah, that's what it is. That's the originality of it. Yeah.
